A5: Carbon Emissions (hello world)¶

For this assignment, you will work with global warming-related datasets. These are Scripps CO2 dataset scripps-co2.csv.bz2 and HadCRUT monthly global temperature hadcrut-monthly.csv. The variables you need and a brief description are written below:

Scripps CO2 Data Set:

year year

month month

co2 (monthly) Mauna Loa observatory CO2 concentration in ppm (particles per million).

HadCRUT Data Set:

year year

month month

anomaly global temperature anomaly in the corresponding month, deg C (corresponding to "baseline," you'll see more info later)

Part I: Loading & Inspecting Data¶

First, let's load the Scripps CO2 data.

In [3]:
scripps <- read.csv("scripps-co2.csv.bz2", sep="\t")
  1. Use glimpse() to make sure the data looks good.

  1. We haven't yet described what the anomaly actually describes; all we know is that it is encoded as a double. Search on Google (or whatever browser or AI engine you use), something along the lines of "hadcrut monthly what is a temperature anomaly." What resource did you use, and what did it say? Does it seem to be a reasonable answer?

Explanation here : A temperature anomaly is the difference between an observed temperature and the average temperature during reference periods. Positive means a warmer than reference average. Seems reasonable because it compares temperature changes over long periods of time.

  1. Now, check your answer with another INFO 201 student to confirm that your search yielded the same or similar results. Which student did you consult, and did your answers match?

Explanation here Xana and our answers were on the same wavelength.

Part II: Advanced dplyr¶

Using the hadcrut dataset and what we know about what the anomaly column means, let's calculate the proportion of months in each decade that had temperature anomalies above or below the average. This analysis will help illustrate long-term patterns and potential evidence of climate change.

For our data set's purposes, we will have all decades starting from the year 1850 until now. Let's first identify that our data set is good in that every decade has 120 months (10 years * 12 months per year). To do this, we created a new decade column as shown below:

In [8]:
hadcrut <- hadcrut |> 
    mutate(decade = year - year %% 10)

Error: object 'hadcrut' not found
Traceback:

1. .handleSimpleError(function (cnd) 
 . {
 .     watcher$capture_plot_and_output()
 .     cnd <- sanitize_call(cnd)
 .     watcher$push(cnd)
 .     switch(on_error, continue = invokeRestart("eval_continue"), 
 .         stop = invokeRestart("eval_stop"), error = NULL)
 . }, "object 'hadcrut' not found", base::quote(eval(expr, envir)))
  1. Inspect the equation in the mutate statement above closely. What does %% mean in the context of the expression above? Write a brief explanation about what this equation does.

Explanation here The %% calculates the remaining after division. When divided by ten its takes away the remainder.

Now we have shown the total number of rows:

hadcrut |>
    group_by(decade) |>
    summarize(months = n())

  1. Why does the row for decade "2020" have only 72 months in it? What does this mean?

Explanation here : It only includes the 2020 - 2025 for 6 years and 12 months per, making 72 months total.

  1. Now, filter this decade out of the data frame. Set this filtered data frame to a variable called hadcrut_subset. Once you've done this, all of our decades in this newly created data frame will contain 120 months.
In [14]:
hadcrut_subset <- hadcrut |>
    filter(decade != 2020)

  1. In the HadCRUT dataset, temperature anomalies are measured relative to a standard reference period, defined in our particular data set as the average temperature from the 1960s to the 1980s (asking ChatGPT or other machines would yield different results because we made some changes to how you use the data set for this assignment). Using this reference period, calculate the average value of the anomaly column for the dataset within these decades and store the result in a variable named avg. You should be using the decade column to achieve this result. Also, because anomalies may be either positive or negative (indicating temperatures above or below the reference average) you should compute avg as the mean of the absolute anomalies. Use as.double() to convert the data frame into a decimal point value. Print avg to show you've done this correctly.

    Hint: to check if a value is in a vector of options (like a set of decades), you can use the %in% operator

    Hint: if you did this correctly, you should see "0.146255555555556" printed. If you're getting a value like "0.138369," then you did the problem incorrectly and should carefully reread the above instructions.

In [15]:
avg <- hadcrut |>
    filter(decade %in% c(1960, 1970, 1980)) |>
    summarize(avg = mean(abs(anomaly))) |>
    as.double()

avg
0.146255555555556
  1. You may observe from the hadcrut dataset that every row has some anomaly value. So, if we group by the decade column and find the proportion of months for each decade where that month's anomaly is more extreme than the average (i.e., the absolute value of the month's anomaly is greater than avg), we might see some indication of global warming. Using the hadcrut data set, do the following:
  • Create a new column above_avg that determines whether the row's absolute anomaly value is greater than the average you computed earlier.
  • Group all rows by the decade.
  • Compute the proportion of months for each decade where the month's anomaly value is greater than the standard reference point average. Call the name of this column prop, which represents the proportion of months whose anomaly value was more extreme than the average.
In [16]:
hadcrut |>
    mutate(above_avg = abs(anomaly) > avg) |>
    group_by(decade) |>
    summarize(prop = mean(above_avg))

Part III: Data Join & ggplot2¶

  1. Let's merge the Scripps and HadCRUT data sets. What variables from each data set would you want to use to merge? Describe the join key.

Explanation here : Use the year and months as join keys, since both have the variables.

  1. Merge these two data sets and save it to a new variable. Use glimpse() to show you did this correctly.
In [17]:
merged <- scripps |>
    inner_join(hadcrut, by = c("year", "month"))

glimpse(merged)

$ anomaly <dbl> 0.258, 0.091, 0.006, -0.068, 0.017, -0.154, -0.018, -0.082, -0…
$ decade  <dbl> 1950, 1950, 1950, 1950, 1950, 1950, 1950, 1950, 1950, 1950, 19…
  1. Do you want to keep all CO2 rows? Do you want to keep all temperature rows? Explain! Note that there is an objectively correct answer for this question.

Explanation here : No I would not keep the CO2 rows or all the temperature now. I would keep where the months and years match.

  1. Make a plot in CO2-temperature anomaly axis. Include the following components.
  • Use the temperature anomaly wrt the pre-industrial average. (use the anomaly column)
  • Mark all months with dots.
  • Mark decades with colors (hint: use factor(decade))
    • You don't have to match our color scheme, but if you want to, we used the color brewer "YlOrRd" (Yellow or Red) palette
  • Ensure that the labels are easy to understand.

You should be using ggplot2 to do this. We added the tidyverse library which includes ggplot.

If you did this correctly, you should see a graph like the following:

In [21]:
ggplot(merged, aes(x = co2, y = anomaly, color = factor(decade))) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd") +
    labs(
        title = "CO2 Concentration vs. Temperature Anomaly",
        x = "CO2 Concentration (ppm)",
        y = "Temperature Anomaly (°C)",
        color = "Decade"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
  1. What is the trend that you notice? Does there seem to be a strong or weak correlation, visually speaking? What could this graph indicate about climate change? Write at least a 50-word statement using full sentences.

Global temperature anomalies and CO2 concentrations have a positive relationship, according to the graph. Temperature anomalies typically rise in line with rising CO2 levels. Despite the fact that certain months have higher or lower temperatures than others, this visually indicates a very significant positive link. This pattern may suggest that rising CO2 levels in the atmosphere are linked to global warming. Although the correlation does not indicate that CO2 is the cause of temperature increases, the graph does support the notion that climate change is taking place.
